findings.issue: Neither source bears on the claimed relationship, which is Benedict's Rule shaping the tenth-century English refounding. Foxe 10969-10971 is about bishops being made by kings, not popes, and fetching their palls from Rome. Gasquet 593-595 is about Middle English translations of the Rule for nuns. Inferential-Thin must carry 'the evidence it rests on'. Here there is none. The note's first two sentences report facts that do not touch the link, and the third admits it. A reader also cannot tell why the three bishops are named. Calling Foxe 'the reformer' is loose; he was the Protestant martyrologist. The tie itself is standard history that has no vendored text. That is the open rule question (era-2 escalation 3, era-4 escalations 2 and 9).
findings.evidence: foxe_acts-and-monuments-v4_cattley-townsend1837.txt 10963-10972; benedict_rule-of-saint-benedict_gasquet1925.txt 588-597; no vendored Regularis Concordia or Æthelwold text (grep of cic/texts).
findings.fix: Do not dress up the link with sources that do not show it. Either (a) hold it out of the edges until Mark rules on the standard-history question, keeping the prose and the wants as they are; or (b) keep it, drop Foxe, and say plainly what it rests on. For example: 'Dunstan, Æthelwold and Oswald are remembered for refounding English monasteries on the Rule of Saint Benedict in the tenth century. No source from their time is cited for this here. A modern editor of the Rule, Cardinal Gasquet, says only that English nuns kept it and had it put into English. So this tie rests on thin evidence.' Set citation_specificity to 'E' for the relationship.

findings.issue: The grade is Contested, which means a live disagreement. The note's last sentence settles it: 'Later studies doubt that the Paulicians were dualists at all, so the line cannot be shown.' It also says more than the cited works are described as holding. The census's own source note on Garsoian says she found that the Greek and Armenian traditions diverge and that the Armenian lacks the dualism, not that the Paulicians were not dualists 'at all'. The drafter flags that neither Garsoian nor Dixon was read. Meanwhile Obolensky (1948) and Stoyanov (2000), both cited in the census for the Bogomils, still argue for Paulician input. The note names only the older side (Rački, Evans) as holding the line.

findings.issue: The note offers Constantine V's move of Paulicians into Thrace as part of the case for 'argued against'. The source it cites says the opposite about motive. Evans writes that Constantine 'had perhaps some sympathies with the heretics' and that the move gave them 'every facility' for their mission. Presented without that, a resettlement under a possibly friendly emperor reads as hostility. The drafter flagged the doubt, and the flag is right. The persecution under Michael I (811-813, Rački) carries the type on its own.
findings.fix: Drop the Constantine V sentence. Or rewrite it: 'Arthur Evans, in 1877, adds that Constantine V moved a body of them from Armenia into Thrace, though he thought the emperor may have favored them.' Keep the Michael I sentence as the core.

10 (Dominant Modern Reconstruction on 19th and early 20th-century works): needs Mark, as a method ruling. My view: for the Paulician and Bogomil links the label is not false, because a current, repo-cited work holds the same reading (Dixon 2022; Obolensky 1948; Stoyanov 2000). Lutzow, Mouravieff and Brosset are different. They retell medieval narratives (the Vita Methodii, the Rus' Primary Chronicle, the Georgian Lives) rather than reconstruct anything, so the label misdescribes what kind of support it is, while the grade itself understates rather than overstates. Dropping them to Inferential-Thin would tell readers that standard facts are thin. A better ruling is either a stated meaning ('rests on secondary works only') or vendoring the medieval texts already listed in wants. The Herberstein inconsistency (R1-02) needs settling either way.
